To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
RFs are able to bind various unrelated structures such as IgG, histones and their fragments, and that the binding site of the RFs is located on the CDR3 region of the VH domain.

(a) the binding sites on histones and IgG recognized by human RFs are distinct; (b) the binding sites recognized by human RF on histones are located in the N-terminus of the histones; (c) the binding sites of human RF on histone H1 and IgG are topographically different; (d) the binding sites for histones H2A and H3 are topographically different from those of H1; (e) the binding sites
RFs recognize histones and IgG through distinct binding sites and that this dual recognition is a common feature of RFs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural basis of double reactivity of RFs.
the structural basis of polyreactive antibodies.
the identification of the histone epitopes involved in the recognition of RFs and with the mapping of the corresponding RF binding sites on the antibody.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the double reactivity for IgG and nucleoproteins of RFs is not due to a single common epitope, but is a result of the recognition by these antibodies of different epitopes located at the N- and C-termini of histones, as well as in the hinge region of IgG.
RFs bind to the N-terminal regions of IgG and histone molecules, and that the IgG binding site is located in the C-terminal region of the molecule.
RFs bind to different regions of histones and to the Fc portion of IgG.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the binding sites of RF for IgG and H1, H2A and H3 histones are not identical, although they overlap to some extent.
the double reactivity is due to the presence on the same molecule of different binding sites for IgG and H1 histone, which are located in distinct regions of the RF molecules.

the double reactivity is not the consequence of the recognition by RFs of a common antigenic determinant present on IgG and histone, but rather of a cross-competition between different sites on these proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the double reactivity for IgG and H1, H2A, H3 histones of the RFs is based on a limited number of epitopes, located in different regions of the proteins and on different topological surfaces.
RFs are able to recognize various regions of the histones, which are not necessarily close in the tertiary structure of these proteins.
the double binding of histones by RFs is not a fortuitous event, but is the consequence of the presence of several epitopes on these proteins, which are recognized by the RF.
